faq.a: Desmopressin has minimal vasoconstrictive effects and is safer for long‑term use in CDI.
faq.q: Why is desmopressin preferred over vasopressin?

faq.a: Yes, dehydration reduces plasma volume, increasing serum sodium and worsening symptoms.
Use clinical criteria and response to desmopressin; a positive response confirms CDI.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with 4 L/day urine and intense thirst. Serum sodium is 158 mmol/L. What is the next best step? — Perform a desmopressin challenge to confirm CDI and start desmopressin if positive.

A patient with suspected CDI has a urine osmolality of 250 mOsm/kg after 8 h water deprivation. What does this indicate? — The low urine osmolality confirms inability to concentrate urine, supporting CDI.
Why is rapid correction of hypernatremia dangerous in CDI? — It can cause cerebral oedema and seizures due to osmotic shift.
A child with polyuria has normal ADH levels. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
What is the first line treatment for CDI in a low‑resource setting? — Desmopressin, preferably intranasal, with careful monitoring of serum sodium.
When should you consider a pituitary MRI in a patient with CDI? — If there is a history of head trauma, pituitary surgery, or if the desmopressin response is atypical.
ai.title: Central Diabetes Insipidus
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: A neurohormonal disorder where ADH deficiency causes large volumes of dilute urine and intense thirst. It is life‑threatening if untreated and common in low‑resource settings due to infections and trauma.

b: Large urine volume (>3 L/day), dilute urine (<300 mOsm/kg), hypernatremia, intense thirst
sections.p: Central diabetes insipidus (CDI) is the failure of the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary to produce or release antidiuretic hormone (ADH). Diagnosis is confirmed by a water‑deprivation test and a desmopressin challenge, showing a marked rise in urine osmolality.

t.b: Assesses ability to concentrate urine; a rise in urine osmolality >50 % after 8 h indicates CDI
Differentiates CDI from nephrogenic DI; a rise in urine osmolality >50 % confirms CDI

sections.p: Severity is staged by serum sodium and volume status. Stage 1: mild hypernatremia (≤150 mmol/L). Stage 2: moderate (151–160 mmol/L). Stage 3: severe (>160 mmol/L) or rapid rise, requiring urgent intervention.
In low‑resource settings, infections, head trauma, and pituitary surgery are common. Other causes include infiltrative diseases and congenital defects.

t.b: Detects pituitary lesions or hypothalamic damage; if unavailable, rely on clinical picture and response to desmopressin

sections.p: Patients report excessive thirst and urination. On examination, they may be dehydrated, with dry mucosa and tachycardia. No specific neurological deficits unless underlying brain injury.

t.b: Shows dilute urine (<300 mOsm/kg) in CDI

sections.p: Key tests are urine and serum osmolality, serum sodium, and a desmopressin challenge. In resource‑poor settings, a simple urine dipstick for specific gravity can be a surrogate.

t.b: Elevated in CDI; a value >150 mmol/L supports diagnosis
Low (<1.005) indicates dilute urine; normal values suggest nephrogenic DI

sections.p: Rapid rise in serum sodium, severe dehydration, or neurological deterioration require immediate care. Complications include seizures, cerebral oedema, and death.

t.b: A rise >10 mmol/L in 24 h signals impending cerebral oedema

b: Close monitoring of serum sodium every 4–6 h
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first. Supportive care includes fluid replacement with hypotonic saline and monitoring. Desmopressin is the drug of choice; avoid over‑replacement to prevent hyponatraemia.

t.b: Mimics ADH; corrects polyuria and hypernatremia
Replaces free water lost; avoid rapid correction

sections.p: Regular monitoring of serum sodium and urine output is essential. Prevent infections and manage head injuries aggressively to reduce CDI risk.

t.b: Tracks urine volume and thirst; helps detect early relapse

b: Nephrogenic DI: no response to desmopressin
sections.p: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, psychogenic polydipsia, and primary polydipsia.

b: Early CDI may have normal sodium
Urine dipstick can over‑estimate specific gravity
sections.p: Serum sodium can be normal early; urine specific gravity may be falsely high if the patient is drinking water. MRI may miss small pituitary lesions.

t.b: May read >1.010 even with dilute urine if sample is contaminated

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypernatremia (>160 mmol/L), rapid rise in sodium (>10 mmol/L in 24 h), neurological deterioration, seizures
